title: Market Order vs Limit Order for Beginners: When to Use Each
meta_description: Market order vs limit order for beginners, in plain English: what happens when you press Buy, worked examples, and when to use each order type.
quick_answer: A market order buys or sells right away at the best price available. You control speed but not price. A limit order fills only at your price or better. You control price, but the order may not fill. Market orders are generally fine for heavily traded large stocks and ETFs during regular hours. Limit orders are safer for thinly traded stocks, the market open, extended hours and volatile news days.
key_takeaways: A market order gets you in or out fast, but you may pay a different price from the last one you saw. This is most likely when the bid-ask spread is wide or prices are moving quickly.
A limit order sets the worst price you will accept. You never pay more, or sell for less, than your limit, but the order may fill only partly or not at all.
Market orders are usually reasonable for heavily traded large-cap stocks and large ETFs during regular hours, when spreads tend to be narrow.
Use limit orders for thinly traded stocks, the first minutes after the open, pre-market and after-hours sessions, and volatile news days.
A stop order becomes a market order when triggered, so it can sell well below your stop if the price gaps. A stop-limit order avoids that but may never fill.
Order types, extended-hours rules and fees vary by broker and country. Before you submit any trade, check your broker's help pages and the order preview screen.
who_this_is_for: This guide is for new investors who have opened a brokerage account, are looking at an order ticket for the first time and want to know what each order type does before they press Buy.
intro: Pressing Buy in a brokerage app feels like one simple action. Behind that button, though, you are choosing an order type. That choice decides whether you get speed, price control or some mix of the two. Most beginners never change the default, and that is usually fine until the day it isn't. That day might bring a thinly traded stock, a hectic market open or an after-hours session where the price you pay ends up well away from the price you saw. This guide explains what happens when you submit an order. It defines the four order types found on most order tickets (market, limit, stop and stop-limit) and walks through a worked example of each, using made-up prices. It also covers when a market order is reasonable, when a limit order is the safer choice, how to place a limit order step by step, and the beginner mistakes worth avoiding. This is general educational information, not trade advice. Your broker's rules, fees and order types may differ from what is described here, so confirm them in your own account.

steps.name: Check the live quote first
steps.text: Open the stock or ETF page and note the bid, the ask, the last price and the day's volume. Work out the spread (ask minus bid). If the spread is wide or volume is low, a limit order is the safer choice.

steps.name: Open the order ticket and choose the action
steps.text: Tap Trade, then Buy or Sell, and check the ticker symbol. Many companies have similar symbols, so make sure the company name matches the one you mean to trade.

steps.name: Set Order Type to Limit
steps.text: Find the field usually labelled Order Type and switch it from Market (often the default) to Limit. A new field called Limit Price will appear.

steps.name: Enter the quantity
steps.text: Type the number of shares in the Quantity or Shares field. Some brokers let you enter a dollar amount instead. Not every broker allows limit orders on fractional shares, so check yours.

steps.name: Choose your limit price
steps.text: For a buy, the limit price is the most you will pay per share. For a sell, it is the least you will accept. A buy limit at or slightly above the current ask usually fills quickly. A buy limit below the ask may get a better price but may not fill at all.

steps.name: Pick the time in force and session
steps.text: In the Time in Force or Duration field, choose Day or Good 'Til Cancelled (GTC). A Day order is cancelled at the end of the session if it hasn't filled. A GTC order stays open until it fills, you cancel it or your broker's expiry limit is reached. If you want the order to work in pre-market or after-hours trading, look for an Extended Hours toggle and read your broker's rules for it.

steps.name: Review the preview and submit
steps.text: On the Review or Preview Order screen, check the action, symbol, quantity, limit price, estimated total, time in force and any fees. Fix anything that looks wrong before you tap Submit or Place Order.

steps.name: Monitor and manage the open order
steps.text: Find the order under Orders, Open Orders or Activity. It will show as open, partially filled or filled. You can usually change or cancel an unfilled order from there. Cancel any GTC order you no longer want so it can't fill unexpectedly later.

sections.heading: What actually happens when you press Buy
paragraphs: When you press Buy, your broker sends your order to an exchange, a market maker or another trading venue. There it is matched with a seller whose price fits the order type you chose.

Every listed stock or ETF has two live prices. The bid is the highest price buyers are currently offering. The ask, also called the offer, is the lowest price sellers will currently accept. The gap between them is the bid-ask spread. The 'last price' shown in large type in your app is simply the most recent trade. It does not guarantee the price of your next trade.

If you buy immediately, you generally pay around the ask. If you sell immediately, you generally receive around the bid. In a heavily traded stock the spread may be a cent or two, so the difference barely matters. In a thinly traded stock the spread can be much wider. Buying at the ask and then selling at the bid could cost you a noticeable amount even if the price hasn't moved.

Each price level also has a size, which is the number of shares available at that price. If you want more shares than are offered at the best ask, the rest of your order fills at the next price up. This is called 'walking the book', and it is one reason a market order can fill at more than one price.
bullets: Bid: the highest price a buyer is offering right now.
Ask: the lowest price a seller is accepting right now.
Spread: the ask minus the bid. A narrow spread usually means plenty of trading activity.
Last price: the most recent trade. It does not promise the price you'll get.

sections.heading: Market, limit, stop and stop-limit orders defined
paragraphs: An order type is the instruction that tells your broker how to trade. The four you will see most often are market, limit, stop and stop-limit, and each balances speed against price control differently.
A market order tells the broker to buy or sell immediately at the best price currently available. In normal conditions it fills almost instantly, but you do not choose the price.

A limit order tells the broker to trade only at a price you set, or better. A buy limit will not pay more than your limit, and a sell limit will not accept less. You control the price, but the order fills only if the market reaches it.

A stop order is called a stop-loss when it is used to sell. It waits until the stock trades at or through a trigger price you choose, called the stop price, and then becomes a market order. Sell stops sit below the current price and are typically used to limit losses on a position you hold. Buy stops sit above the current price.

A stop-limit order also waits for a stop price, but once triggered it becomes a limit order rather than a market order. You set two prices: the stop price that activates the order and the limit price, which is the worst price you will accept.
bullets: Market: fast, but the price is not guaranteed.
Limit: you get your price or better, but the order may not fill.
Stop: triggers at a set price, then trades as a market order.
Stop-limit: triggers at a set price, then trades as a limit order.

sections.heading: Worked examples of each order type (made-up prices)
paragraphs: The examples below use an imaginary company, Example Co., with invented prices. They show how each order behaves. None of the numbers describes a real security or suggests a trade.

Market order: Example Co. shows a bid of $50.00 and an ask of $50.05, and you place a market order to buy 10 shares. If at least 10 shares are offered at $50.05, you pay about $500.50 before fees. If only 5 shares are offered at $50.05 and the next 5 are at $50.10, your order fills at both prices, for an average of $50.075 per share. If the price moves between your tap and the fill, the result could be different again.

Limit order: The quote is the same, and you place a buy limit for 10 shares at $49.80. Nothing happens until sellers will trade at $49.80 or lower. If the price dips there, your order may fill at $49.80 or better. If the price climbs to $52.00 instead, the order sits unfilled. You haven't overpaid, but you don't own the shares either. You could also get a partial fill, such as 6 of your 10 shares.

Stop order: You own 10 shares bought at $50.00 and place a sell stop at $46.00. If the stock trades at $46.00, the order becomes a market order and might sell at $45.95. Now suppose bad news comes out overnight and the stock opens at $42.00. Your stop triggers at the open and sells at around $42.00, not $46.00. A stop order does not protect you from a gap like this.

Stop-limit order: You hold the same position but set a stop of $46.00 and a limit of $45.50. If the stock drifts down to $46.00, the order becomes a sell limit at $45.50. It should fill at $45.50 or better if buyers are there. If the stock opens at $42.00 instead, the order triggers but can't fill, because nobody is paying $45.50. You still hold the shares, and the price may keep falling or may recover. The order protected your price but didn't get you out.

sections.heading: When a market order is usually fine
paragraphs: A market order is usually fine for small orders in heavily traded large-cap stocks or large, popular ETFs during regular market hours. Spreads in these securities tend to be narrow, and plenty of shares are offered near the quoted price. The gap between the price you see and the price you get is usually small.

This is why many long-term investors who buy a broad-market fund every month use market orders without trouble. The convenience is real. The order fills and you are done, with no unfilled order left hanging.

'Usually fine' is not 'always fine', though. A market order on any security can fill at a surprising price during a sudden sell-off, when trading resumes after a halt, or right at the open. If a fill noticeably different from the quote would upset you, place a limit order near the current ask. It gives you nearly the same speed with a price ceiling.
bullets: Large, widely held companies with high daily trading volume.
Large ETFs with narrow, stable spreads.
Regular trading hours. To be cautious, avoid the first and last few minutes.
Orders that are small compared with the shares available at the quoted price.

sections.heading: When to use a limit order instead
paragraphs: Use a limit order whenever the price you could end up paying is uncertain. The main cases are thinly traded stocks, the market open, extended-hours sessions and volatile news days. In each, spreads can widen and prices can jump, and a limit order caps your worst-case price.

Thinly traded stocks, including many small-cap and micro-cap shares, often have wide spreads and few shares at each price. A market order can walk up through several price levels and fill well above the last trade.

The market open is often busier and more volatile than the rest of the day, because orders that built up overnight are processed and prices adjust to overnight news. Spreads can be wider for the first few minutes.

Pre-market and after-hours sessions usually have far fewer participants, which can mean wider spreads and bigger swings. Many brokers accept only limit orders during extended hours, and session times and eligible securities vary by broker.

Earnings releases, major economic announcements and company headlines can move prices between the moment you see a quote and the moment your order reaches the market. A limit order stops that movement from pushing your fill past a price you have set.
bullets: Thinly traded or small-cap stocks with wide spreads.
The first minutes after the opening bell.
Pre-market and after-hours trading.
Earnings days and other major news events.
Larger orders that could use up all the shares offered at the best price.

sections.heading: Market order vs limit order for beginners: how to decide
paragraphs: To choose between a market order and a limit order, ask yourself one question. Would a fill noticeably different from the quote I see right now be a problem for me? If not, and you are trading a heavily traded security in regular hours, a market order is a reasonable choice. If it would be a problem, or you are unsure, use a limit order.

Many beginners take a middle path. When buying, they set a limit at or slightly above the current ask. When selling, they set it at or slightly below the current bid. In liquid markets this usually fills about as fast as a market order, and it protects you if the price jumps while the order is in transit.

Setting the limit far from the current price is a different strategy. You may get a better price, but the order may never fill, and you could miss the trade entirely. Neither result is right or wrong. What matters is choosing on purpose instead of accepting the default.

Order type only controls how a trade is executed. It does not make an investment more or less suitable for you. What to buy, how much and for how long depend on your goals, time horizon and risk tolerance. For personal decisions, consider speaking with a licensed financial adviser.
bullets: Liquid security, regular hours, small order and speed matters: a market order is generally reasonable.
Wide spread, low volume, extended hours or a news-driven move: a limit order is generally safer.
Unsure: a limit order near the current ask (buy) or bid (sell) gives you speed with a price cap.

sections.heading: Common beginner mistakes and a pre-trade checklist
paragraphs: Most order-type problems come from a few avoidable mistakes, and a short checklist helps you catch them before you submit.

Forgotten GTC orders are a common trap. A Good 'Til Cancelled buy limit set weeks ago can fill on a sudden dip after you have changed your mind or spent the cash. Review your open orders regularly and cancel anything you no longer intend to trade.

A limit price set on the wrong side of the market quietly removes your protection. A limit means 'this price or better', so a buy limit typed far above the ask normally fills near the ask. A sell limit far below the bid normally fills near the bid. Either way, the order behaves much like a market order, so read the limit price on the preview screen carefully.

A stop set very close to the current price can be triggered by ordinary daily swings and sell a position you meant to keep. Another common surprise comes from placing an order outside regular hours with the Extended Hours setting switched off. The order then waits for the next session and may fill at a different price from the one you saw.
To make the checklist a habit, keep it somewhere you will actually see it. A phone note, a spreadsheet or a workspace tool all work. Copy the template below and run through it before every order.
bullets: Symbol and company name match what I intend to trade.
I have checked the bid, ask, spread and today's volume.
I chose market or limit on purpose, not by default.
My limit price is the worst price I'm willing to accept.
Time in force (Day or GTC) and the Extended Hours setting are what I want.
The preview shows the right quantity, estimated total and fees.

sections.heading: Fees, risks and broker rules to check before you trade
paragraphs: Before placing any order, check your own broker's order types, fees and session rules, because they differ between brokers and countries. This article describes how these orders generally work. It cannot guarantee how your broker handles them.

Fees can include commissions, charges on certain order types or markets, currency conversion fees for foreign shares, and regulatory fees on sales in some countries. A broker may advertise zero-commission trading, but the spread and the way your order is routed still affect your total cost. Your broker's fee schedule and order preview screen show what you will actually pay.

Order-handling rules vary too. Some brokers allow only market orders for fractional shares. Some convert large market orders into limit orders with a price 'collar' to prevent extreme fills. GTC orders often have a maximum duration, and stop orders may be triggered by brief price spikes or by different reference prices.

All investing carries risk, including losing the money you invest, and no order type removes that risk. Trading rules, investor protection and tax treatment differ by country. For your specific situation, check your local financial regulator's investor education resources or speak with a licensed adviser.
bullets: Read your broker's help pages on order types and time-in-force options.
Confirm extended-hours session times and which order types are allowed in them.
Check the fee schedule, including currency conversion and any charges for particular order types.
Always review the order preview before you submit.

recommendations.best_for: Beginners who want to keep their pre-trade checklist and a simple trade journal in one place. The journal can record order type, limit price, fill price and the reason for each trade, so you can learn from how your orders actually filled.
recommendations.not_for: Anyone looking for trading features. Notion does not place orders, connect to brokers for execution or provide market quotes. A free spreadsheet or paper notebook works just as well for a checklist or journal, and features and pricing change, so check Notion's site before signing up.

faq.question: Is it bad for a beginner to use market orders?
faq.answer: No. Market orders are a normal tool and are generally reasonable for heavily traded large-cap stocks and large ETFs during regular trading hours. The risk comes from using them on thinly traded stocks, at the open, in extended hours or during fast-moving news, when the fill price can differ noticeably from the quote.

faq.question: What happens if my limit order doesn't fill?
faq.answer: If the market never reaches your limit price, the order stays open until it expires or you cancel it. A Day order is usually cancelled at the end of the trading session. A Good 'Til Cancelled order can stay open longer, up to your broker's maximum. The order can also fill partly, with the rest staying open.

faq.question: Should I use a market or limit order to buy an ETF?
faq.answer: For large, heavily traded ETFs during regular hours, both types generally work, and many investors use a limit near the current ask for extra protection. Smaller or niche ETFs can have wider spreads, which makes a limit order the safer choice. Check the bid, ask and volume on the quote screen before you decide.

faq.question: Can I use a market order in pre-market or after-hours trading?
faq.answer: Many brokers accept only limit orders during extended-hours sessions, because trading is thinner and spreads can be much wider. Rules vary by broker. Check your broker's extended-hours policy, session times and eligible securities before placing an order outside regular hours.

faq.question: What is the difference between a stop order and a stop-limit order?
faq.answer: Both wait for a trigger price called the stop price. A stop order then becomes a market order and fills at the next available price, which can be well past the stop if the price gaps. A stop-limit order becomes a limit order, so it won't fill below your limit, but it may not fill at all.

faq.question: Do limit orders cost more than market orders?
faq.answer: At many brokers the commission is the same for both, but not everywhere. Some brokers charge differently depending on order type, market or account type. Check your broker's fee schedule and the estimated costs on the order preview screen.

conclusion: The choice between a market order and a limit order comes down to what matters more on a given trade: speed or price. Market orders fill fast and are generally fine for heavily traded large-cap stocks and large ETFs during regular hours. Limit orders protect your price and are the safer choice for thinly traded stocks, the market open, pre-market and after-hours sessions, and volatile news days. Stop and stop-limit orders add a trigger price, but neither guarantees your exit price. Before your next trade, open your broker's order ticket and find the Order Type, Limit Price and Time in Force fields. Read the broker's help pages on extended hours and fees, and run through the pre-trade checklist above. This article is general information, not trade advice. For decisions about your own money, check your local regulator's guidance or speak with a licensed adviser.
